displayQuote: Once You Are Dead, You Are Made for Life

meta.title: Who really said "Once You Are Dead, You Are Made for Life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jimi Hendrix really said it — to Melody Maker on 8 March 1969, eighteen months before he died. Not a deathbed line, and the printed wording has no comma.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Once You Are Dead, You Are Made for Life'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Hendrix said it in a Melody Maker interview published 8 March 1969 — not shortly before his death. Quote Investigator confirmed it from scans.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Hendrix said it to Bob Dawbarn of the British weekly Melody Maker, in an interview published on 8 March 1969 — eighteen months before his death, not on any deathbed. Quote Investigator ↗ verified the passage against scans of the issue; the wording as printed is “Once you are dead you are made for life,” with no comma.

source.heading: Melody Maker, 8 March 1969

docMeta.dd: “Third Dimension: Hendrix the Man” — interview by Bob Dawbarn
8 March 1969 — article begins page 12, quotation on page 13

source.excerpt: It’s funny the way most people love the dead. Once you are dead you are made for life. You have to die before they think you are worth anything.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the line to Melody Maker of 8 March 1969 — Bob Dawbarn’s interview, beginning on page 12 with the quotation on page 13 — and states it verified the issue from scans obtained through interlibrary loan.
The official Hendrix chronology ↗ independently records the sitting: Dawbarn of Melody Maker interviewed Hendrix in London on 26 February 1969 for feature articles published on 1 and 8 March.

Chris Welch, a Melody Maker colleague, reprinted the passage in his Hendrix biography; Open Library holds the catalogue record for that Flash Books edition of 1973 ↗, which Quote Investigator cites at page 32.

Wikiquote’s Hendrix page ↗ does not carry this line at all — not as sourced, attributed, disputed or misattributed — so Quote Investigator’s dossier stands as the only substantive investigation of it.
source.excerptNote: The passage does not end there. In the same interview Hendrix went on to say he wanted a jam session rather than a funeral, with his own music played loud — the part of the conversation that almost never travels with the epigram.

source.rightsNote: The words were first published in Melody Maker on 8 March 1969 — comfortably inside copyright in the United States — so the interview as printed belongs to the paper’s publisher, which Quote Investigator’s citation records as IPC Specialist & Professional Press of London. Hendrix’s own music, name and likeness passed to Experience Hendrix, L.L.C. ↗, the family company founded by his father Al Hendrix in 1995; quoting a sentence here for identification and comment is a separate matter from reproducing the article.

author.name: Jimi Hendrix
author.heading: Jimi Hendrix
author.bio: Born Johnny Allen Hendrix in Seattle on 27 November 1942 and later renamed James Marshall Hendrix, he was the guitarist, singer and songwriter who redefined what an electric guitar could be made to do. He died in London on 18 September 1970, aged 27. The Melody Maker conversation that produced this line catches him in a sardonic mood about the music business — in the same interview he complained that the trade sees a fast buck and turns the performer into a slave to the public.

cite.sourceCitation: Bob Dawbarn, “Third Dimension: Hendrix the Man” (interview with Jimi Hendrix), Melody Maker, 8 March 1969, 12–13; quotation on page 13. Reprinted in Chris Welch, Hendrix: A Biography (New York: Flash Books, 1973), 32.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Once You Are Dead, You Are Made for Life’?” Last verified 7 Sep 2026.

copyAttribution: “It’s funny the way most people love the dead. Once you are dead you are made for life.” — Jimi Hendrix, interviewed by Bob Dawbarn, Melody Maker, 8 March 1969. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with it
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is seriously credited with this line — there is no rival claimant anywhere in the record. What circulation gets wrong is when he said it, how he said it, and where the sentence stops.

items.why: The reader who wrote to Quote Investigator ↗ had it this way, and most retellings still do. The interview ran on 8 March 1969, eighteen months before Hendrix died on 18 September 1970, and was conducted in London on 26 February 1969 according to the official Hendrix chronology ↗.

items.who: “Once you’re dead, you’re made for life”
items.why: The contracted form is the one quote sites carry, and it is not what the paper printed: Melody Maker ran “Once you are dead you are made for life,” without contractions and without the comma. Quote Investigator ↗ notes that some instances in circulation have slightly altered wording; the comma’d version matches the 1988 UPI printing rather than the 1969 original.

In print the thought does not stop at the punchline. It runs on to a third sentence — that you have to die before anyone thinks you are worth anything — and sits inside a complaint about a business that Hendrix said turns a performer into a slave to the public, as Quote Investigator ↗ shows from the 1969 text and Chris Welch’s 1973 reprint.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is sound: Hendrix said it, to Bob Dawbarn, in Melody Maker of 8 March 1969, verified from scans of the issue by Quote Investigator ↗. What needs correcting is the deathbed framing and the tidied-up wording, not the name on it.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: It travels as a prophecy. Search it today and you will usually find it introduced as something Hendrix said shortly before he died — the doomed guitarist at 27, staring down his own myth. That framing is the one thing about it that is definitely wrong. He said it to a music paper on an ordinary Wednesday in a three-part feature interview, and what he was actually complaining about was the industry: that recognition arrives too late, and that the trade will happily sell an artist harder dead than alive.

Then he died eighteen months later, and the joke became an epitaph. Quote Investigator ↗ reports that in the same conversation Hendrix said he wanted a jam session instead of a funeral, with his own music played loud — which is the part of the interview that reads far stranger now than the epigram everybody quotes.
context.detailsSummary: How the line got from a 1969 music weekly to every quote site
detailsBody: The route is short and traceable. Chris Welch, a colleague of Dawbarn’s at Melody Maker, reprinted the passage in his Hendrix biography — the Flash Books edition of 1973 ↗, on page 32 according to Quote Investigator’s citation — which put it in front of readers who would never see a 1969 back issue.

In 1988 United Press International ran it as the thought for the day in its syndicated “Today in History” column, in the comma’d form “Once you are dead, you are made for life.” From newspaper filler it passed into quote databases, where it usually loses the comma-free 1969 phrasing, loses the third sentence, and gains a deathbed.
context.pull: He was needling the record business in 1969. Eighteen months later the joke turned into an epitaph.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the quotation to Melody Maker of 8 March 1969, an interview of Jimi Hendrix by Bob Dawbarn (start page 12, quote page 13, IPC Specialist & Professional Press, London), verified with scans via interlibrary loan; prints the wording "It's funny the way most people love the dead. Once you are dead you are made for life. You have to die before they think you are worth anything."; records that the interview appeared eighteen months before Hendrix's September 1970 death; that Hendrix said he would have a jam session rather than a funeral; that Chris Welch reprinted it in a 1973 Flash Books biography at page 32 along with the "slave to the public" remark; that UPI's "Today in History" carried it in 1988 with a comma; and concludes the quotation appears authentic while noting some circulating instances have slightly altered wording.

The Official Jimi Hendrix Site's encyclopedia entry states: "February 26, 1969 London, England — Bob Dawbarn of Melody Maker interviews Hendrix for a series of features articles that are published on March 1 and March 8."

Jimi Hendrix was born Johnny Allen Hendrix on 27 November 1942 in Seattle, Washington, later renamed James Marshall Hendrix; he died on 18 September 1970 in London, England, aged 27; he was a guitarist, singer and songwriter.
Melody Maker was a British weekly music publication established in January 1926 and ceased publication in December 2000; its publisher is identified as IPC Media.

Wikiquote's Jimi Hendrix page contains no entry for "Once you are dead you are made for life" or "It's funny the way most people love the dead" in any section, and no citation to Melody Maker 1969 — verified by reading the full page.
Open Library's catalogue record shows Chris Welch's Hendrix biography published by Flash Books in 1973.

Experience Hendrix, L.L.C. was founded by Al Hendrix in 1995 as a Seattle-based company to handle the estate, after Al Hendrix gained control of his son's legacy including his music, name and likeness; it is led with his adopted daughter Janie Hendrix.
